parties:
Alamgir Hossain (Md) alias Alamgir ----- Convict-Petitioner.
Vs.
State  ----- Opposite Party.
full_judgment:
Mahmudul Amin Choudhury J: This Rule was issued calling upon the Deputy Commissioner, Gazipur to show cause why the order of conviction and sentence passed by the learned Special Tribunal No.3, Gazipur in Special Tribunal Case No. 33 of 1991 convicting the petitioner under sections 4(c) and 9 of the Cruelty to Women (Deterrent Punishment) Ordinance, 1983 and sentencing to suffer imprisonment for 10(ten) years with a fine of Taka 5,000.00 should not be set aside. 

 2. The short fact leading to this Rule is that, one Khadiza Khatun lodged FIR with Joydebpur Police Station on 15-5-1984 alleging that for providing the informant with better employment the petitioner took the informant to Joydebpur and thereafter to Dhaka where she was detained against her will and there she also found two other girls who were also brought for sending them to Pakistan. It is also the case of the informant that for better security she was taken to Gopibag area of Dhaka and confined there against her will and there this petitioner had illicit and forcible intercourse with her. Subsequently when pressure was put on the mother of the petitioner by the parents of the informant she was taken to Tongi and then to Joydebpur. Her father then took her with him. The police on receipt of the FIR took up investigation of the case and ultimately submitted chargesheet. This petitioner was then placed on trial before the Tribunal who found him guilty of the accusation under section 376 of the Penal Code read with section 4(c) and 9 of the Cruelty to Women (Deterrent Punishment) Ordinance. 1983 and sentenced to suffer rigirous imprisonment for 10(ten) years with fine as aforesaid. 

 4. At the time of issuance of the Rule it was brought to our notice that two conflicting decisions have been given by two different Benches of this Division reported in 15 BLD 239 and 46 DLR 175, as regards the authority of this Court on the question of entertaining and disposing of an application filed under section 561 A of the Code of Criminal Procedure where the convict failed to avail of the forum of appeal as contemplated under section 30 of the Special Powers Act and the matter was referred to the Hon'ble Chief Justice for constituting a larger Bench and accordingly, the present Bench for disposal of the matter was constituted. When the matter was taken up for disposal we felt the necessity of assistance from the Senior Members of the Bar and accordingly we requested Senior Advocates Mr Abdul Malek, Mr M Nurullah and Me Khondker Mahbub Hossain to address the Court on the points involved in the case as Amici Curiae which they accepted. 

 5. It appears from the perusal of the record that this petitioner was arrested in connection with this case on 25-6-1984 and was enlarged on bail on 15-7-1984 and thereafter he absconded. His bail was cancelled on 2-2-88. But he never surrendered before the Tribunal or before any other Court The Tribunal found this petitioner guilty and convicted and sentenced him as aforesaid by judgment dated 25-4-1995. Then the petitioner was arrested by the police on 22-6-95 and the present petition was filed on 23-7-1995. 

 6. Mvi Md Wahidullah, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the accused-petitioner at the very outset submits that it is a case of no evidence. It is submitted that in the petition of complaint or before the Tribunal it has not been alleged by the informant on which date she was raped by the petitioner. There is also no medical evidence to prove the factum of rape and how she was recovered. As regards the point of law involved Mvi Md Wahidullah submitted that the case being under a Special Law and the petitioner having not availed of the forum of appeal he may invoke the inherent jurisdiction of this Court under section 561A of the Code of Criminal Procedure and when there is no legal evidence adduced from the side of the prosecution this Court may in its inherent jurisdiction interfere in the matter and quash the conviction. 

 In support of his submissions Mvi Md Wahidullah placed reliance on the case of Sher Ali and others vs. State, reported in 46 DLR (AD) 67 where it has been held that the inherent powers conferred under section 561A of the Code of Criminal Procedure may be invoked independent of powers conferred by any other provisions of the Code. It has also been held that this power may be exercised to quash a proceeding or even a conviction on conclusion of trial if the Court concerned got no jurisdiction to hold the said trial or the facts alleged against the accused do not constitute any criminal offence, or the conviction has been based on no evidence or otherwise to secure the ends of justice. The Appellate Division in arriving at this decision also followed the case of Mofazzal Hossain Molla vs. State, reported in 45 DLR (AD) 175. Mvi Wahidullah submits that in the present case before us the facts alleged against the accused has not constituted any criminal offence and the conviction has been based on no evidence and as such this Court may interfere under section 561A of tile Code of Criminal Procedure. 

 7. He also placed reliance in the case of Sohail Ahmed Chowdhury vs. State reported in 15 BLD 452 where it has been held by the High Court Division that although the inherent power of the High Court Division under section 561A of the Code of Criminal Procedure is generally exercised for preventing an abuse of the process of the Court in respect of a pending proceeding but nevertheless the said power can also be exercised in respect of a proceeding which has reached its finality after the conclusion of the trial when it is found necessary to prevent an injustice. It has also been held that this power should be exercised sparingly and in exceptional cases where the offence alleged do not constitute any criminal offence or conviction has been based on no legal evidence or shockingly inadequate evidence. Basing his arguments on these two decisions Mvi Wahidullah submits that the prosecution failed to produce any evidence to find the guilt of the petitioner. 

 8. Mr Abdul Malek, the learned Counsel appearing as Amicus Curiae also submits that for invoking the inherent power under section 561A of the Code of Criminal Procedure this Court may follow the principle of law enunciated in 46 DLR (AD) 67 which has clearly spelt out the authority of this Division in the matter of interference in such cases. Me Abdul Malek also placed the case of Abdul Quader Chowdhury and others vs. State reported in 28 DLR (AD) 38, where it has been held that in a case where the allegations made against the accused do constitute an offence alleged but there is either no legal evidence adduced in support of the case or the evidence adduced clearly or manifestly fails to prove the charge. In dealing with this class of cases it is important to bear in mind the distinction between a case where there is no legal evidence or where there is evidence which is manifestly and clearly inconsistent with the accusation in question. 

 9. Supporting the submissions made by Mvi Md Wahidullah, Mr Malek submits that this Court may interfere in the matter under section 561A of the Code of Criminal Procedure as the evidence adduced failed to substantiate the accusation framed against the petitioner. He also submits that the accusation have been framed against the petitioner under section 376 of the Penal Code, but there is no medical evidence to prove the factum of rape. It is submitted that it is incumbent on the prosecution to prove the factum of rape by medical evidence or the evidence of the chemical examiner which is very much absent in the present case Mr Malek contends that the contention of the informant who deposed as PW 1 has not been corroborated by any other evidence and in such circumstances this Court may interfere under section 561A of the Code of Criminal Procedure. In Support of his submission Mr Abdul Malek placed reliance in the case of Muhammad Abdul Khaleque & others vs. State, reported in 12 DLR (SC) 165 where it has been held that before finding an accused person guilty of rape, that is of sexual intercourse without the consent of the woman, the Court should .be satisfied that the woman's story is corroborated either by circumstantial evidence connecting the accused-person with the crime, or that at least by some 'circumstances connected with the woman which would serve by itself to show that her story of forcible intercourse is true. It has been held that the mere fact of the story having been told to a number of relations shortly after the occurrence is insufficient corroboration. Equally, the fact of the story having been communicated by the relations to other neighbours and later to the authorities is by no means sufficient corroboration. 

 10. Mr M Nurullah the learned Counsel also as Amicus Curiae, on the other hand, submits that the High Court cannot make any order in exercise of its inherent powers under section 561A of the Code of Criminal Procedure if it will result in granting relief to a party for which statutory remedy is barred by time. The scope of jurisdiction of the High Court under section 561A of the Code of Criminal Procedure may certainly be wider than its revisional jurisdiction under section 439 of the Code of Criminal Procedure in certain respects, a mere irregularity in the procedure which does not justify the interference in criminal revisions will not normally justify the interference with the course of trial of a case in exercise of the inherent jurisdiction of the Court under section 561A of the Code of Criminal Procedure. Mr Nurullah in support of his submission placed reliance in the case of S. Gurdial Singh & others vs. Abhey Dass, reported in A I R 1967 (Punjab) 244. 

 11. Mr. Nurullah also placed reliance in the case of Muhammad Samiullah Khan and another vs. State, reported in 15 DLR (SC) 150 where it has been held that in the exercise of inherent jurisdiction under section 561A of the Code of Criminal Procedure the High Court can neither exercise the powers of a Court of appeal nor can it enhance sentence nor can it even re-consider the question of sentence. It is designed to prevent an abuse of the process of Court and cannot be regarded as being wide enough to give to the High Court the same power that it has under section 435 read with section 439 of the Code of Criminal Procedure to examine the correctness, legality or propriety of any finding, sentence or order passed by an inferior Court. Mr. Nurullah submits that the forum provided for in preferring appeal is within 30 days from the date of the order of conviction and sentence and when the petitioner failed to avail of that opportunity he cannot invoke this Court's inherent jurisdiction. In support of his submission Mr. M Nurullah took us to the Indian Jurisdiction in the case of Dharma Pal, reported in 1993 (SC) 435, wherein it has been held that the" inherent powers of the Court cannot be utilised for exercising powers which are expressly barred by the Code. He submits that the Special Law created a bar for preferring appeal beyond 30 days from the date of the order of conviction and sentence and as such the petitioner cannot invoke the jurisdiction of this Court under its inherent power. It is also submitted that inherent power under section 561A of the CrPC being extraordinary and residuary power, is not available with regard to the matter which has been specifically provided for under other provisions of law. The High Court may not exercise its inherent power where any party could have or did not avail of the remedy of revision. He placed reliance on the principle of law reported in 1986 CrLJ (Allahabad) 1233 (Avadh Narain Lal Vs. State. 

 12. Mr. M Nurullah placing the decision of Pakistan Supreme Court reported in 1967 PLD (SC) 317 (Ghulain Muhammad vs. Muzzamal Khan and others) submits that the inherent jurisdiction given to the Court under section 561A of the Code of Criminal Procedure is not an alternative jurisdiction or an additional jurisdiction. Rut it is a jurisdiction preserved in the interest of justice to redress grievance for which no other procedure is available or has been provided by the Code itself. Without controverting the principle of law enunciated by our Appellate Division in the case of Sher Ali and others vs. State, reported in 46 DLR (AD) 67, Mr Nurullah submits that in the present case the petitioner was arrested by police on 25-6-84 and thereafter he was favoured with bail on 15-7-84 and the bail was cancelled on 2-2-88. The petitioner it appears was fully aware of the proceeding against him and he came out of the custody on furnishing a bail bond promising that he will attend the Court from where he was released and also promising to attend the transferee Court but he deliberately avoided appearance before the Court and remained absconding and allowed the case to be disposed of in his absence. Even after the disposal of the case he has not voluntarily surrendered but was arrested on 22-6-95 and then he filed this application before this Court invoking the inherent jurisdiction. Mr Nurullah submits that such a litigant is not entitled to highly discretionary relief. A person who deliberately and wilfully avoided the proceeding and allowed the case to be disposed of in his absence may not be favoured with any highly discretionary relief. It is also submitted that for invoking this Court's inherent jurisdiction an accused-person or a convict should approach the Court with clean hands. But the facts and circumstances in the present case indicate that the petitioner moved this Court with unclean hands and, as such, he may not be favoured with, any relief. 

 13. As regards the submission of Mvi Md Wahidullah that there is no legal evidence in support of conviction Mr Nurullah contends that this Court sitting under section 561A of the Code of Criminal Procedure cannot appreciate or deal with the evidence. It is the function of the trial Court or the appellate Court. Mr Nurullah submits that the evidence as adduced indicates that the petitioner had illicit intercourse with the informant against her will and that has been corroborated by another witness to whom she reported after she was rescued. He submits that his statement is sufficient to hold that the petitioner has committed the offence punishable under section 4(c) of the Cruelty to Women(Deterrent Punishment) Ordinance. He also submits that in a case punishable under section 4(c) of the Cruelty to Women (Deterrent Punishment) Ordinance the prosecution is not obliged to prove the factum of rape as contemplated under section 376 of the Penal Code. Section 4(c) of the Cruelty to Women (Deterrent Punishment) Ordinance is self explanatory where it has been provided that whoever kidnaps or abducts any woman of any age in order that such woman may be forced or seduced to illicit intercourse or knowing it to be likely that she will be forced or seduced to illicit intercourse shall be punishable with imprisonment for life, etc. Mr Nurullah submits that the informant is not the legally married wife of the petitioner and any intercourse with her by anybody including the petitioner excepting her husband is illict intercourse and the evidence disclosed that the informant was seduced to go to Gopibag on a promise that she would be given better employment and there the petitioner taking advantage of her position without her consent had illicit intercourse with her which comes very much within the ambit of section 4(c) of the Cruelty to Women (Deterrent Punishment) Ordinance. Mr Nurullah placing the provision of section 373 of the Penal Code submits that the word 'rape' used in the section is not equal to the word 'illicit sexual intercourse' used in section 4 (c) of the Cruelty to Women (Deterrent Punishment) Ordinance. 

 14. Mr Khondker Mahbub Hossain appearing as Amicus Curiae submits that there is a scope for interference by this Court under section 561A of the Code of Criminal Procedure in the case of this nature when the provision of the Code of Criminal Procedure is not inconsistent with the provision of the Special Law. He submits that section 561A of the Code of Criminal Procedure is not inconsistent with any provisions of the Special Powers Act or Cruelty to Women (Deterrent Punishment) Ordinance. It is submitted that in the present case before us as there is no evidence against this petitioner this Court may interfere under section561A of the Code of Criminal Procedure. In support of his submission Mr Khondker Mahbub Hossain placed reliance in the case of Kamruzzaman vs. State, reported in 42 DLR (AD) 219 wherein the provision of section 339C of the Code of Criminal Procedure has been made applicable in the case instituted under the Special Powers Act as the provision of section 339C of the Code of Criminal Procedure is not in- consistent with the provision of the Special Powers Act. So, for securing the ends of justice this Court may act under its inherent jurisdiction when there is no evidence against the petitioner. He submits that the question has been set at rest by our Appellate Division in the case reported in 46 DLR (AD) 67 and that is the latest decision on the subject in question. 

 15. Mr MA Rouf, learned Assistant Attorney-General appearing on behalf of the State adopting the submission made by Mr M Nurullah, submits that the petitioner has not agitated this petition on the ground that the Tribunal had no jurisdiction to try and dispose of the case and when the Tribunal has acted within the jurisdiction its findings and decision of guilt may not be interfered with under section 561A of the Code of Criminal Procedure as there is evidence against this petitioner. He submits that sufficiency or insufficiency of evidence cannot be agitated in a petition of this nature which is the function of the trial Court as well as of the appellate Court. He also submits that had it been a petition under section 439 of the Code of Criminal Procedure then there might have been some scope for examining the evidence. But as this petition is a petition under section 561A of the Code of Criminal Procedure there is no scope for examining the evidence. He submits that the petitioner was fully aware of the proceeding against him but he deliberately avoided the proceeding and obtained his bail which disentitled him a relief under section 561A of the Code of Criminal Procedure. 

 17. This Special Bench was constituted to thrash out the question which has been raised in view of the decisions reported in 46 DLR 175 (Mir Mohammad Ali vs Md Giasuddin). In this decision it has been held that section 561A of the Code of Criminal Procedure has not given any new jurisdiction to the High Court to override other laws. It is easy to say that this Court cannot have any inherent jurisdiction to strike down the law of limitation. In that case the petitioner failed to avail of the provision of appeal and as it was barred under the law that the appeal should be preferred within 30 days from the date of judgment and order. But as the convict failed to prefer appeal within time and as section 5 of the Limitation Act has no manner of application the petitioner in that case filed the petition under section 561A of the Code of Criminal Procedure. It has been held that the law of Limitation is not inexorable that a person loses his good title on account of law of limitation and that it may be desirable that something is done for the redress of the accused who lost his right of appeal and has a very good case in their defence. In that case it has been propounded that section 561A of the Code of Criminal Procedure cannot be conceived of to give the High Court jurisdiction to retrieve the cases from the moratorium after they have been barred by limitation. 

 18. In the case of Sohail Ahmed Chowdhury vs. State reported in 15 BLD 452 a Division Bench of this Court has held that although the inherent power of the High Court Division under section 561 A of the CrPC is generally exercised for preventing an abuse of the process of the Court in respect of a pending proceeding but nevertheless the said power can also be exercised in respect of a proceeding which has reached its finality after the conclusion of the trial when it is found necessary to prevent an injustice. But this power should be exercised sparingly and in exceptional cases where the facts alleged do not constitute any criminal offence or conviction has been based on no legal evidence or shockingly inadequate evidence. In the said case the petitioner earlier preferred Criminal Appeal No. 713 of 1990 before the High Court Division which was found to be barred and thereafter on a petition filed by the convict petitioners the same was converted into Criminal Miscellaneous Case No. 944 of 1995 under section 561A of the Code of Criminal Procedure and then the final order was passed. 

 19. From these two aforesaid decisions it appears that a convict who failed to prefer appeal within statutory period cannot invoke the inherent jurisdiction of this Court as propounded in 46 DIR 175 whereas in 15 BLD 452 case the opposite view has been taken, that is, the same may be interfered with under the inherent jurisdiction of this Court and that is the reason behind the constitution of the Special Bench. 

 21. But it is well settled that this inherent jurisdiction of the court should be exercised sparingly and in exceptional cases. In the case before us no objection has been raised from the petitioner that the Tribunal has no jurisdiction to hold the trial. There is also no allegation that the facts alleged do not constitute any criminal offence against the petitioner. The FIR disclosed a criminal case. The only contention from the side of the petitioner is that there is no legal evidence. Both Mvi Md Wahidullah and Mr Abdul Malek submitted that the present case is a case of no evidence. It appears that in the FIR and before the Court the informant specifically stated that this petitioner had illicit intercourse with her against her will and the evidence disclosed a case against this petitioner. It is well settled that sitting in this jurisdiction under section 561A of the Code of Criminal Procedure this Court cannot appreciate or shift the evidence adduced from the side of the prosecution. So, it cannot be found that there is no evidence in this case. The petitioner has failed to substantiate his case that there is no evidence against him before the Tribunal. 

 22. In view of the consistent decision of the Higher Courts of the sub-continent and particularly the decision of our Appellate Division, reported in 46 DLR (AD) 67 the scope of such an application is very narrow and it appears that the petitioner failed to substantiate that the Tribunal had no jurisdiction and the facts alleged do not constitute any criminal offence and the conviction has been based on no evidence. It appears that the petitioner was charged under section 376 of the Penal Code read with section 4(c) of the Cruelty to Women (Deterrent Punishment) Ordinance section 4(c) of the Ordinance providing that whoever kidnapa or abducts any woman of any age in order that such woman may be forced or seduced to illicit intercourse or knowing it to be likely that she will be forced or seduced to illicit intercourse may be punished. Here in the present case the informant who was promised to be provided with better employment was taken to Gopibag, Dhaka where against her will the petitioner had illicit intercourse with her and the allegation definitely comes within the provisions of section 4 (c) of the Ordinance as admittedly the informant is not the legally married wife of the petitioner and any intercourse with her is illicit intercourse and there is also allegation that she was seduced to or forced to illicit intercourse by the petitioner. 

 23. As regards the objection raised by Mr Abdul Malek that as there is no supporting medical evidence the accusation may be taken as not proved. But in a case punishable under section 4(c) of the Cruelty to Women (Deterrent Punishment) Ordinance medical evidence is not a must if the allegation can be proved otherwise. 

 24. So, from a consideration of the materials on record and after hearing the learned Counsels, we are of the view that the petitioner has failed to make out any case for our interference under section 561A of the CrPC. 

 25. Here in the present case it appears that the petitioner was arrested by police on 25-6-1984 and was bailed out on 15-7-85 and thereafter he absconded and his bail was cancelled on 2-2-1988 and he remained absconding till his re-arrest on 26-2-95 after the judgment was delivered by the Tribunal and then he moved this Court and obtained the present Rule. 

 Now in such circumstances the question is whether the petitioner may invoke the jurisdiction of this Court under section 561A of the Code of Criminal Procedure. It is well-settled that this power of the Court is to be exercised sparingly and in exceptional cases and this exceptional extraordinary power is to be exercised in cases which has been filed by diligent persons and one who comes with clean hands. In the case of 46 DLR (AD) 67 the petitioner faced the trial and also preferred appeal which was dismissed and then within time he moved the learned Sessions Judge in revision and which was also rejected and moved the High Court Division under section 561A of the Code of Criminal Procedure which was summarily rejected and then he went to the Appellate Division and got the result in his favour. The petitioner of that case was always vigilant and he approached the Court with clean hands. But here in the present case before us this petitioner misused the privilege of bail and remained absconding allowing the case to be disposed of in his absence and then after the statutory period of filing appeal he preferred this application under section 561A of the Code of Criminal Procedure. 

 The petitioner has failed to make out any case for our interference and he is a defaulting person who approached this Court with unclean hands and, as such, he is not entitled to any discretionary relief. 

 26. Having given our anxious consideration to the materials on record and after hearing the learned Advocate of both the sides, we are of the view that the dispute in question as rasied in 46 DLR 175 and 15 BLD 239 has been set at rest by the decision of our Appellate Division, reported in 46 DLR (AD) 67. A convict may invoke the jurisdiction of this Division under section 561A of the Code of Criminal Procedure if he can make a case of coram non-judice of the trial Court or that the facts alleged do not constitute any criminal offence or the conviction has been based on no evidence or otherwise to secure the ends of justice arid with that we add that he should approach the Court with clean hands. The petitioner failed to make out any case as aforesaid. 

 Before we conclude we must record our appreciation for the assistance rendered by the learned Amicus Curiae who took great pains and trouble in addressing the Court on the legal points as well as on the factual side of the present case. We appreciate their services to this Division for the sake of administration of justice.
